title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE GENITIVE OF ABSENCE, TURNED ON A PERSON. M3 taught net plus the genitive for a thing that is not here; a person who is not here takes exactly the same shape, and M2's yevó and yeyó are already genitive. Yevó net dóma, Yeyó seychás net. Three modules, one construction — and a learner who meets it a third time as a new idiom has learnt nothing from the first two.

Russian answers the phone with Alló and identifies with Éhto Iván — the same "this is" move English makes. Ya Iván sounds like an introduction at a door, which is the mistake to expect. Éhto is L1-M1's own word doing its own job, so nothing new is opened for it.

ASPECT ON THE PHONE, and it is the level's third payment. Ya vam pozvonyú is perfective — one call, a promise. Ya búdu vam zvonít' is the imperfective future — I'll be calling, repeatedly. The pair shows what L1-M6 could only assert: the perfective has NO present tense, which is why pozvonyú is a future and not "I am calling".

REGISTER ON THE PHONE is a rule about not knowing rather than about politeness: vy is the default even with someone you would ty in person, because you do not know who has picked up. So this module is written in vy throughout, and M6's ty is deliberately absent from it.
A message is taken with Chto peredát'? and passed on with On zvoníl — the past L1-M6 already owns. On skazál, chto… is reported speech and belongs to L3; nothing here reaches for it.

words.note: Only on the phone. Zdrávstvuyte is for meeting someone; alló is for answering, and using either in the other place is heard at once.
The other way of answering, and slightly more formal. Literally "I am listening", which is what an office says instead of alló.

sentences.trap: Ya Iván is what a learner reaches for and it sounds like an introduction at a door. On a phone Russian says Éhto Iván, exactly as English says "this is".
sentences.sound: a-LO. Both l's are hard and the stress is on the second syllable — the word is not said the way English "hello" is.

variations.changed: a different name
the more formal answer
identifying someone else

mistake.why: On the phone Russian uses éhto: Alló! Éhto Iván.

sentences.usage: Picking up, or opening a call you have made.
sentences.mnemonic: alló is only ever a phone.

sentences.cue: May I speak to Anna, please?

words.note: The accusative of a name. Feminine names in -a take -u; a masculine name is animate, so its accusative looks like its genitive — Ivána.
A telephone number, a hotel room, a size — one word for all three. Its plural moves the stress to the ending: nomerá.

sentences.trap: M1's mózhno again, with no verb after it. The name is an accusative, so a feminine one changes: Ánna becomes Ánnu, and a masculine name would not move at all.
sentences.sound: MOZH-na AN-nu pa-ZHA-lsta. The double n is held slightly longer than a single one, which is audible in Russian and not in English.

variations.cue: May I speak to Ivan, please?
variations.changed: a masculine name — animate, so its accusative does move

variations.cue: May I speak to your brother?
variations.changed: a relative rather than a name
what is said when the number is wrong

mistake.why: The person asked for is an object: Mózhno Ánnu, pozháluysta?

sentences.usage: Asking for someone when a third person answers.
sentences.mnemonic: mózhno plus an object, no verb needed.

words.cue: to pass on · to take (a message)
words.note: The infinitive of M5's peredáyte. Chto peredát'? is what a Russian says where English says "can I take a message?" — and it too has no subject.

sentences.trap: This is M3's Zdes' net magazína with a person in it, and yevó was already genitive when M2 taught it. Nothing new has happened, which is exactly the point.
sentences.sound: yi-VO nyet DO-ma. The g of его is a v, and net takes a beat of its own.

variations.cue: She's not here at the moment
variations.changed: the feminine, and a time word

variations.cue: He's not here. Can I take a message?
variations.changed: the whole exchange in one line
the feminine

mistake.why: The absent person goes in the genitive: Yevó net dóma.

sentences.usage: Answering a call for someone who is out.
sentences.mnemonic: Absent people go in the genitive too.

sentences.cue: Can I take a message? I'll write it down

words.note: The noun, used mostly of a written or recorded message. A spoken one passed on by a person is simply peredát' — the verb, not the noun.
L1-M6's napishú with a different prefix: za- means down onto something. Perfective, so it is a future — the rule that makes aspect visible.

sentences.trap: Chto peredát'? has no subject and no "can I". It is a bare question word plus an infinitive, and it is the whole of what a Russian says here.
sentences.sound: shto pi-ri-DAT'? ya za-pi-SHU. chto is said shto, which L1-M9 established and which never varies.

variations.changed: the question alone
a named thing to write down
the noun rather than the verb

mistake.why: The fixed question is short: Chto peredát'?

sentences.usage: Offering to take a message. Two words, and nobody expects more.
sentences.mnemonic: Question word plus infinitive, no subject.

words.cue: to call (repeatedly, or as an activity)
words.note: The imperfective partner of pozvonít'. It has a present tense — ya zvonyú, I am calling — which the perfective does not, and that is the diagnostic.
pozvonyú with pere- on the front, which adds "back" or "again" — the same prefix as M5's peredáyte.

sentences.trap: pozvonyú is a promise of ONE call, and it is a future only because the perfective has no present. Ya búdu vam zvonít' means something else — I'll be calling, more than once.
sentences.sound: ya vam paz-va-NYU VYE-chi-ram. The verb runs to its last syllable, which is where the whole sentence lands.

variations.changed: the prefix that means back
a different time
the imperfective past — the fact of a call, not its result

mistake.why: pozvonít' takes the dative: Ya vam pozvonyú vécherom.

sentences.usage: Closing a call you cannot finish now.

words.note: Perfective, because waiting a moment is one act. Its ty form podozhdí shares this row — one verb, two addresses, as M6's rule 4 set out.
A diminutive of minúta, and the diminutive is what makes it friendly rather than curt. Russian softens by shrinking the noun, where English adds a word.

sentences.trap: Russian softens this request by making the minute SMALLER, not by adding please — though please is there too. That is a move English has no equivalent for, and it runs through the whole language.
sentences.sound: pa-dazh-DI-tye mi-NUT-ku pa-ZHA-lsta. The zhd cluster is said as written, with no vowel between.

variations.changed: without the minute
without the verb — and complete
the ty address, to a friend

mistake.why: The waited time is an object: Podozhdíte minútku, pozháluysta.

sentences.usage: On the phone, at a counter, in a doorway.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian softens by shrinking the noun.

sentences.cue: Tell me your phone number, please

words.note: The genitive telefóna is doing M3's "of" job — number of telephone. Two nouns side by side, and the second one carries the of.
The vy possessive, beside M2's moy. It agrees with what is owned, never with the owner — vash nómer whoever is being addressed.

sentences.trap: nómer telefóna is a genitive, exactly like M4's ostanóvka avtóbusa. Once the pattern is seen, every "X of Y" in the language is the same shape.
sentences.sound: ska-ZHI-tye vash NO-mir ti-li-FO-na. Three unstressed vowels in telefóna, all reduced to something near i.

variations.changed: shorter, and enough on a phone
the answer, with M2's possessive

variations.cue: I'll write down your phone number
variations.changed: the whole thing as an object

mistake.why: The second noun goes in the genitive: nómer telefóna.

sentences.usage: Exchanging numbers, which in Russian is done with this exact question.
sentences.mnemonic: X of Y: the Y goes genitive.

words.note: Hearing rather than listening — slúshayu is the deliberate one. Russian keeps them apart where English can use "hear" for both.

sentences.trap: Russian says "I do not hear you", where English says "I can't hear you". There is no mózhno or mogú in it, and adding one makes the sentence sound like a complaint about permission.
sentences.sound: iz-vi-NI-tye ya vas nye SLY-shu. The y of slýshu is the hard back vowel, and the sh in front of it forces it further back still.

variations.changed: without the apology
the question, and the pronouns swap
understanding rather than hearing

mistake.display: Izviníte, ya ne mogú vas slýshat'
mistake.script: Извините, я не могу вас слышать
mistake.why: Russian says it plainly: Izviníte, ya vas ne slýshu.

sentences.usage: On a bad line — and it is heard as a fact about the line, not a complaint about the speaker.
sentences.mnemonic: No "can" in it. Just "I don't hear".

words.note: The imperfective past: a call happened. L1-M6's pozvoníl is the perfective and says the call got through — the difference is result, not length.

sentences.trap: This is how a message is passed on, and no reported speech is needed. On skazál, chto… exists and belongs to L3; here the fact of the call is the whole message.
sentences.sound: on zva-NIL vam U-tram. The past ending -l is barely more than a touch of the tongue.

variations.changed: a woman, so the past agrees with her
the perfective — the call got through
a different time

mistake.why: The past agrees with the subject: On zvoníl vam útrom.

sentences.usage: Telling someone who rang while they were out.
sentences.mnemonic: The past agrees with whoever did it.

words.note: A whole surface, and another genitive of wishing like M5's Príyatnogo appetíta. Neither of its words is opened, because the frame behind them is L3's.

sentences.trap: A Russian call ends with more words than an English one, not fewer. Ending on spasíbo alone is heard as cutting someone off, and do svidániya is the minimum.
sentences.sound: kha-ra-SHO spa-SI-ba da svi-DA-ni-ya. The whole closing runs as one long fall.

variations.changed: the warmer closing
without the thanks
a promise on the way out

mistake.why: Poká is for friends; a vy call ends with do svidániya.

sentences.usage: Ending a call. The closing is longer than an English one and skipping it is noticed.
sentences.mnemonic: A call ends on more words, not fewer.
